questions.q: What is the correct order of the five-question connectivity diagnostic sequence in this lesson?
options: Listening, resolving, allowed, routed, running
Running, routed, allowed, resolving, listening
Allowed, running, listening, routed, resolving
There is no fixed order — check whichever layer seems most likely first
questions.explain: The sequence moves from the broadest, cheapest check (is it running) to the narrowest, most specific one (is the service listening on the right port).

questions.q: Why does the sequence check 'is there a route to it' before checking firewall/NSG rules?
options: Because firewall rules are checked first in every other course
Because route tables are always the actual cause of connectivity problems
Because it's a broader, cheaper check that should be ruled out before narrowing in on a more specific rule-level cause
Because routing and firewall rules are actually the same thing
questions.explain: The order moves broad to narrow — confirming a path exists at all is cheaper and more fundamental than checking the specific rule governing one port.

questions.q: In the worked walkthrough, the ticket passes 'running' and 'routed' but fails at 'allowed.' What should happen next?
options: Reboot the resource, since a failed NSG check usually means a crashed VM
Stop there — the NSG/security group rule gap already explains the entire symptom
Assume the ticket is unsolvable and escalate immediately
Continue checking DNS resolution anyway, just to be thorough
questions.explain: The sequence is designed to stop at the first failing question — there's no value in checking DNS or the listening port once the firewall layer already explains the whole ticket.

questions.q: Why does the sequence check DNS resolution with a tool like nslookup or dig before assuming the IP address itself is wrong?
options: Because DNS is always the first thing to check, before confirming the resource is running
Because a hostname can resolve to an old or incorrect IP even when the underlying resource and network path are both fine
Because DNS never actually causes connectivity failures
Because nslookup fixes DNS problems automatically
questions.explain: Confirming what IP a hostname actually resolves to rules out a whole category of "wrong destination" problems before you start debugging the IP-level connection itself.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say running the five questions out of order usually costs more time, not less?
options: Because the five questions must be run in a random order for the results to be valid
Because this lesson recommends skipping straight to the fix without diagnosing at all
Because jumping to a hunch (like checking app logs first) can waste time investigating a layer that was never reachable due to an earlier, unchecked layer
Because out-of-order checks always produce the wrong answer
questions.explain: Both Lesson 31's and Lesson 32's real incidents resolved quickly specifically because the broad, cheap checks ran before the narrower, more time-consuming ones.
